Short answer
- The difference (B − A) is a bias in the residual stream that pushes early-token continuations toward professional/credential and culinary/cooking vocabulary. In other words, Model B is more likely than A to continue with tokens like "dissertation", "doctoral", "professional"/"professionalism", "Innovation"/"innovative", and cooking/restaurant words ("culinary", "cooking", "Cook", "Restaurant", "Cake", "microwave", "baking") — especially at the first few token positions (pos1 is the strongest) and encoded in later layers.

Why I conclude that
- Spatial pattern: the L2 norm is concentrated in later layers (layers ~10–25) and strongly at token position 1 (p1 dominates from layer 10 onward), so the effect is on early next-token planning encoded late in the network.
- Logit-lens evidence: the high-norm cells consistently point to a small set of thematic tokens across many layers/positions: "dissertation", "doctoral", "professional"/"Professional"/"professionalism", "Innovation"/"innovative", and many culinary terms ("culinary", "cooking", "Cook", "Restaurant", "Cake", "microwave", "baking", "oven", etc.). These clusters show the same semantic directions appear repeatedly in the difference vectors.
- The pattern is robust across many layers and positions (not a single stray cell), so this is a systematic shift in what early residual activations favor.

Limits / caveats
- I cannot identify a precise training objective or dataset from this alone. The shift could come from fine-tuning on professional bios/resumes, journalism about achievements/innovation, restaurant/recipe/cooking text, or any mixture that elevates those tokens. The evidence supports naming a semantic bias (professional/credential + culinary) but not a single definitive cause.
